## Pronunciation

- {替|tì} tì and {提|tí} tí (HSK 3: {提起|tí qǐ}, lesson 11): fourth tone for "in place of", second for "to lift, to mention".
- {={系|jì}=} jì (to tie) vs {={系|xì}=} xì (department) and {关系|guān xi} guān xi: three readings of one simplified character
  (traditional {=繫, 系 and 係=}). Tie = jì.
- {贵姓|guì xìng} guì xìng: two fourth tones. {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ rises at the end only a little: it's a question word-free question.
- {恭喜|gōng xǐ} gōng xǐ: first tone, then third. {恭喜|gōng xǐ}{恭喜|gōng xǐ} is said quickly, gōng xǐ gōng xǐ.
- {赠送|zèng sòng} zèng sòng: *z* and *s*, both fourth tone; {增|zēng} zēng (to increase) is first tone.
- {醉|zuì} zuì and {最|zuì} zuì (most) sound the same.
- {握|wò} wò (to grip) and {我|wǒ} wǒ (I) differ only in tone.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{贵姓|guì xìng}{安|Ān}~~: {贵|guì} is for the other person. Say {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{安|Ān}.
- ~~{一|yí}{副|fù}{鞋|xié}~~: shoes take {双|shuāng}: {一|yì}{双|shuāng}{鞋|xié}. {副|fù} is for glasses, gloves and sets.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{亲自|qīn zì}{刷牙|shuā yá}~~: {亲自|qīn zì} stresses that someone took the trouble personally; for everyday things, say {自己|zì jǐ} or nothing.
- ~~{朝|cháo}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí}~~: abstract directions take {向|xiàng}: {向|xiàng}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí}, {向|xiàng}{你|nǐ}{道歉|dào qiàn}.
- {系|jì}{领带|lǐng dài} is jì lǐng dài, not xì lǐng dài.
- {替|tì} is "instead of, on behalf of": {我|wǒ}{替|tì}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} means you won't have to call. To call someone, {给|gěi}{他|tā}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}.
- Don't open a present the moment it's handed over unless the giver asks you to; say {谢谢|xiè xie}, {您|nín}{太|tài}{客气|kè qi}{了|le}.

## Key points

- {替|tì} + person + verb: for, instead of, on behalf of ({替|tì}{我|wǒ}{问|wèn}{好|hǎo}, {替|tì}{你|nǐ}{高兴|gāo xìng}, {替|tì}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}).
- {亲自|qīn zì}: in person, taking the trouble oneself ({罗教授|Luó jiào shòu}{亲自|qīn zì}{做|zuò}{菜|cài}).
- {朝|cháo} (physical direction, facing) and {向|xiàng} (also abstract: {向|xiàng}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí}).
- {朵|duǒ} (a flower, a cloud), {束|shù} (a bunch), {副|fù} (a pair, a set: {眼镜|yǎn jìng}, {手套|shǒu tào}; shoes take {双|shuāng}).
- {别|bié} bié: to pin; {={系|jì}=} jì: to tie ({系|jì}{领带|lǐng dài}).
- {亲朋好友|qīn péng hǎo yǒu}: friends and relatives (formal), as subject or object.
- {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？—{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}…; {欢迎|huān yíng}{光临|guāng lín}; {恭喜|gōng xǐ}; {改天|gǎi tiān}{再|zài}{来|lái}; {一点儿|yì diǎnr}{心意|xīn yì}.
- Post: {邮局|yóu jú}, {邮票|yóu piào}, {信封|xìn fēng}, {住址|zhù zhǐ}, {贴|tiē}, {邮寄|yóu jì} (written), {询问|xún wèn} (written), {前来|qián lái} (formal); {小姐|xiǎo jie} with care.
- New characters: {憾|hàn} {奈|nài} {肃|sù} {赞|zàn} {传|chuán} {副|fù} {恭|gōng} {替|tì} {贴|tiē} {册|cè} {握|wò} {摇|yáo} {局|jú} {赠|zèng} {醉|zuì}.

lessons.title: Zheng He's voyages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module has been about people: friends, families, guests and hosts. Its first honors lesson
follows a man who spent much of his life as a guest in other people's countries and a host to
their envoys: {郑和|Zhèng Hé} Zhèng Hé (Zheng He), who led the great fleets of the early Ming dynasty across the
Indian Ocean. You'll read who he was, where the fleets went, what they carried, and what is still
argued about. Words outside the course are glossed where they come and listed at the end.

## Who was Zheng He?

Zheng He was born in about 1371 in Yunnan ({云南|Yún nán} Yún nán), in China's south-west, into a Muslim
family; his family name was {马|Mǎ} Mǎ (Ma), and he was known as {马和|Mǎ Hé} Mǎ Hé. As a young man he served
the Ming prince who became the Yongle Emperor ({永乐|Yǒng lè} Yǒng lè, reigned 1402–1424), and rose to be one
of his most trusted officials. He was given the new surname {郑|Zhèng}.

## Seven voyages, 1405–1433

In 1405 the Yongle Emperor sent Zheng He to the "Western Ocean" ({西洋|Xī yáng} Xī yáng): to the Chinese of
the time, the seas and lands to the south and west of China, from today's South-East Asia to the
Indian Ocean. Between 1405 and 1433 he led seven voyages, most of them lasting about two years.

| Voyage | Years (dates from the sources below) | Farthest places reached (as reported) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1405–1407 | Calicut, on India's south-west coast |
| 2 | 1407–1409 | Calicut |
| 3 | 1409–1411 | Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and the Indian coast |
| 4 | 1413–1415 | Hormuz, on the Persian Gulf |
| 5 | 1417–1419 | Malindi, on the coast of East Africa |
| 6 | 1421–1422 | Aden, Mogadishu |
| 7 | 1431–1433 | Hormuz (part of the fleet went on to Aden and the African coast) |

The fleets called at ports all round the ocean: Champa (in today's Vietnam), Java, Sumatra and
Malacca, Ceylon, the Indian coast, the Arabian peninsula and East Africa. Zheng He died on the seventh voyage or soon
after it: most sources give 1433, some a year or two later, and they differ on where. After that voyage, the Ming court sent no
more great fleets.

## The fleets and the "treasure ships"

The numbers are huge for the time. For the first voyage, the figures usually given are about
27,800 men and between about 250 and over 300 ships (sources differ), among them 62 large "treasure
ships" ({宝船|bǎo chuán} bǎo chuán, "treasure boats": {宝|bǎo} is lesson 13's character). On board were sailors and
soldiers, doctors, and interpreters.

How big the treasure ships were is disputed. Ming records give dimensions that would make the
largest well over 100 metres long; many historians doubt that wooden ships of the time could be so
big and suggest something much smaller, around 50 to 70 metres. There is no agreed answer.

## What travelled, and what was written down

The fleets carried silk ({丝绸|sī chóu} sī chóu), porcelain ({瓷器|cí qì} cí qì) and tea, and gifts from the emperor to
foreign rulers. They brought back spices, medicines, gems, fine cloth, and animals unknown in China.
During the fourth voyage a giraffe ({长颈鹿|cháng jǐng lù} cháng jǐng lù), a gift from the ruler of Bengal, arrived at
court (a painting of it survives), and people compared it with the qilin ({麒麟|qí lín} qí lín), a lucky animal
of legend; later voyages brought animals from East Africa too, giraffes among them. Envoys from many countries came back with the fleets to visit the Ming
court.

One of the interpreters, {马欢|Mǎ Huān} Mǎ Huān (Ma Huan), sailed on three of the voyages and wrote a book about
the countries he saw, 《{瀛涯胜览|Yíng yá shèng lǎn}》 (*Yíng yá shèng lǎn*, roughly "Wonders of the Ocean Shores"),
finished and published later, in 1451. In 1431, before the last voyage, stone inscriptions were
set up at Liujiagang and at Changle, near the coast, recording the earlier voyages.

Historians still discuss why the voyages were made (trade, diplomacy, a show of the empire's power)
and why they stopped. The lesson leaves those debates to them; the facts above are the ones the
sources agree on.

## Reading: the seven voyages

1. Where was the "Western Ocean" for the people of the time?
2. How many people sailed on the first voyage, according to the history books?
3. What do the old books and today's historians disagree about?
4. Why did people rush to see the giraffe?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. The seas south and west of China and the lands nearby: today's South-East Asia and the Indian Ocean ({指|zhǐ}{的|de}{是|shì}{中国|Zhōng guó}{南|nán}{边|biān}{和|hé}{西|xī}{边|biān}{的|de}{大|dà}{海|hǎi}{和|hé}{附近|fù jìn}{的|de}{地方|dì fang}).
2. More than twenty thousand ({两万|liǎng wàn}{多|duō}{人|rén}), on more than two hundred ships.
3. How big the treasure ships were ({宝船|bǎo chuán}{到底|dào dǐ}{有|yǒu}{多|duō}{大|dà}).
4. It looked like the qilin of the old books ({觉得|jué de}{它|tā}{很|hěn}{像|xiàng}{古书|gǔ shū}{里|lǐ}{说|shuō}{的|de}"{麒麟|qí lín}").

"More than six hundred years ago, in Ming China, there was a famous navigator called Zheng He.
Zheng He was born in Yunnan in about 1371, and his family name was originally Ma. As a young man
he served a prince who later became the Yongle Emperor, and Zheng He became one of the emperor's
most important men. In 1405 the
Yongle Emperor sent Zheng He with a great fleet from China to the 'Western Ocean'. What people
then called the 'Western Ocean' meant the seas south and west of China and the lands nearby,
that is, today's South-East Asia and the Indian Ocean. From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He made seven
voyages to the Western Ocean altogether, each time spending about two years at sea, reaching South-East Asia, India and the Arabian
peninsula, and at the farthest, the east of Africa. Zheng He's fleet was enormous. The history
books say that on the first voyage there were more than two hundred ships and more than twenty
thousand people. On board were sailors, soldiers, doctors and interpreters. The biggest ships
were called 'treasure ships'. But how big were they really? What the books say differs from the
view of many historians today, and there is still no agreed answer. The fleet took a great deal
of porcelain, silk and tea, and brought back from many places spices, medicines, local products,
and animals no one in China had ever seen. Wherever the fleet
arrived, Zheng He presented the emperor's gifts to the local ruler, and many countries sent envoys
back to China with the fleet. One year the fleet brought back a giraffe, and people
rushed to see it, thinking it looked just like the qilin of the old books. Ma Huan, who went to
sea with Zheng He, recorded the people and things he saw in every country, and later made a book
of them, the *Yingya Shenglan*. Today we can still learn from it about life in the countries of
the seas at that time. Zheng He died on his last voyage or soon after his return. His
seven voyages are a very important page in the history of Chinese navigation."
</details>

lessons.title: Lijiang and the Dongba script
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

China has many writing systems besides Chinese characters. One of the most remarkable is the
Dongba script ({东巴文|Dōng bā wén} Dōng bā wén) of the Naxi ({纳西族|Nà xī zú} Nà xī zú), whose home is around the town of
Lijiang ({丽江|Lì jiāng} Lì jiāng) in the north-west of Yunnan province. Its signs look like little pictures,
and it is still read today by a small number of specialists. This lesson describes the script,
the manuscripts written in it, and the old town of Lijiang. Words outside the course are glossed
where they come and listed at the end.

## A script of pictures

Dongba writing is mostly **[[pictographic]]** ({象形|xiàng xíng} xiàng xíng): many of its signs are drawings of what they
mean, a person, a horse, a mountain, water, the sun. Other signs stand for sounds, and signs are
combined to make ideas. Counts of the number of signs differ with the source and with what is
counted: about 1,400 in some descriptions, more than 2,000 in others.

The script was written by the **dongba** ({东巴|dōng bā}), the ritual specialists of the Naxi religious
tradition (the word gives the script its name). They wrote with bamboo pens and ink they made themselves, on a
tough local paper, in long narrow books. The texts are mostly for ceremonies: prayers, blessings,
funerals, divination, the stories of how the world began; they also record knowledge of the
calendar, farming and daily life.

A Dongba text doesn't write down every word. The signs record the key words and ideas of a passage,
and a reader who has learned the text recites it in full; a single sign may prompt a whole phrase.
The Naxi also have a second script, a syllabic one called Geba ({哥巴文|Gē bā wén} Gē bā wén), which is sometimes
written alongside.

## Manuscripts and a world register

The nomination to UNESCO speaks of some 20,000 volumes of Dongba manuscripts kept in Lijiang, in
other Chinese libraries and museums, and in collections in Europe, America and Japan. In 2003 the
**Ancient Naxi Dongba Literature Manuscripts** were inscribed on UNESCO's **Memory of the World**
Register, a list of documents of world importance. The nomination described the tradition as at
risk: few dongba who can read the old books are still alive, and efforts are being made to teach the
script to younger people.

## The old town of Lijiang

The Old Town of Lijiang, with the nearby villages of Baisha ({白沙|Bái shā}) and Shuhe ({束河|Shù hé}: {束|shù} is lesson 15's
character), became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, the year after a strong earthquake in the
area (February 1996). The town is known for its stone-paved lanes, its wooden houses, and the
streams that run through it, crossed by many small bridges; its history goes back several
centuries (sources date the town from about the 13th century; some speak of a thousand years).
Today it also draws a great many visitors.

## Reading: Lijiang and the Dongba script

> 2003{年|nián}，{纳西|Nà xī}{东巴|dōng bā}{古籍|gǔ jí}{被|bèi}{列入|liè rù}{了|le}{联合国教科文组织|Lián hé guó Jiào kē wén zǔ zhī}{的|de}《{世界记忆名录|Shì jiè Jì yì Míng lù}》。{可是|kě shì}，{今天|jīn tiān}{能|néng}{读|dú}{懂|dǒng}{这些|zhè xiē}{经书|jīng shū}{的|de}{东巴|dōng bā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{了|le}。{为了|wèi le}{让|ràng}{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{文字|wén zì}{不|bù}{消失|xiāo shī}，{丽江|Lì jiāng}{有|yǒu}{一些|yì xiē}{学校|xué xiào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{教|jiāo}{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{学习|xué xí}{东巴文|Dōng bā wén}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{年轻|nián qīng}{人|rén}{也|yě}{对|duì}{它|tā}{产生|chǎn shēng}{了|le}{兴趣|xìng qù}。
>
> {如今|rú jīn}，{走|zǒu}{在|zài}{丽江|Lì jiāng}{古城|gǔ chéng}{的|de}{小|xiǎo}{街|jiē}{上|shàng}，{你|nǐ}{还|hái}{能|néng}{在|zài}{商店|shāng diàn}{的|de}{牌子|pái zi}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}{到|dào}{东巴文|Dōng bā wén}。{这些|zhè xiē}{可爱|kě ài}{的|de}"{小|xiǎo}{图画|tú huà}"，{让|ràng}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{游客|yóu kè}{觉得|jué de}{既|jì}{新鲜|xīn xiān}{又|yòu}{亲切|qīn qiè}。{有的|yǒu de}{游客|yóu kè}{还|hái}{会|huì}{买|mǎi}{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{用|yòng}{东巴文|Dōng bā wén}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}{自己|zì jǐ}{名字|míng zi}{的|de}{卡片|kǎ piàn}，{带|dài}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{做|zuò}{纪念|jì niàn}。

New words: {铺|pū} pū (to pave), {传统|chuán tǒng} (traditional, lesson 25), {记忆|jì yì} (memory, lesson 16), {代表|dài biǎo} (to stand for,
lesson 03), {音|yīn} (a sound, a syllable), {弯弯|wān wān}{的|de}{线|xiàn} (curving lines), {活着|huó zhe} (alive), {宗教|zōng jiào} zōng jiào (religion), {主持|zhǔ chí}{仪式|yí shì}
(to lead a ceremony: {主持|zhǔ chí} is lesson 24's, {仪式|yí shì} HSK 6), {经书|jīng shū} (scriptures, religious books), {天文|tiān wén} (astronomy),
{历法|lì fǎ} (calendar-making), {农业|nóng yè} (farming, lesson 24), {整段话|zhěng duàn huà} (a whole passage), {念|niàn} (to read aloud, lesson
18), {古籍|gǔ jí} (old books), {列入|liè rù} (to be included in), {联合国教科文组织|Lián hé guó Jiào kē wén zǔ zhī} (UNESCO), 《{世界记忆名录|Shì jiè Jì yì Míng lù}》 (the Memory of
the World Register), {产生|chǎn shēng}{兴趣|xìng qù} (to become interested), {牌子|pái zi} (a sign, a board), {做|zuò}{纪念|jì niàn} (as a souvenir: {纪念|jì niàn}, lesson 25), {既|jì}…{又|yòu}… (both… and…,
HSK 4).

1. What is the old town of Lijiang like?
2. How does Dongba writing show "water"?
3. What is unusual about the way Dongba texts are written?
4. What is being done so that the script won't disappear?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. A town several hundred years old, with stone-paved lanes, wooden houses, many streams and small stone bridges.
2. With a few curving lines ({画|huà}{几|jǐ}{条|tiáo}{弯弯|wān wān}{的|de}{线|xiàn}，{就是|jiù shì}"{水|shuǐ}").
3. Not every word is written: only the most important ones, and the reader recites the whole passage from memory ({只|zhǐ}{写|xiě}{最|zuì}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{字|zì}，{读|dú}{的|de}{人|rén}{要|yào}{靠|kào}{记忆|jì yì}{把|bǎ}{整段话|zhěng duàn huà}{念|niàn}{出来|chū lái}).
4. Some schools in Lijiang have begun teaching it to children, and many young people have become interested ({丽江|Lì jiāng}{有|yǒu}{一些|yì xiē}{学校|xué xiào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{教|jiāo}{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{学习|xué xí}{东巴文|Dōng bā wén}).

"Lijiang is in the north-west of Yunnan province in China, an old town several hundred years
old. The lanes of the old town are paved with stone, and on both sides are old houses,
most of them made of wood. Many streams flow through the old town, crossed by many small stone
bridges. In 1997 the Old Town of Lijiang became a World Heritage Site. Lijiang is where the Naxi
live. The Naxi have a very special script, called 'Dongba writing'. Dongba writing looks like
pictures: draw a person, and it means 'person'; draw a few curving lines, and it's 'water'; draw a
mountain, and it's 'mountain'. Some people call Dongba writing 'a pictographic script
that is still alive in the world'. There are different accounts of how many signs it has: some say over a
thousand, some over two thousand. The Naxi have another script too, called 'Geba writing', in
which each sign stands for a syllable; it is sometimes written together with Dongba. Dongba writing was mainly written by the dongba, the people who
lead ceremonies in the traditional Naxi religion. They wrote scriptures with pens made of bamboo,
on paper made locally. This paper doesn't wear out easily, so many of the books have survived to
this day. These books record many ancient stories, and knowledge of astronomy, the
calendar, farming and daily life. Interestingly, Dongba writing doesn't write out every word, only
the most important few, and the reader relies on memory to recite the whole passage. In 2003 the
ancient Naxi Dongba manuscripts were included in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. But today
very few dongba can still read these books. So that the script doesn't disappear, some schools in
Lijiang have begun teaching it to children, and many young people have become interested in it
too. Today, walking along the lanes of the old town, you can still see Dongba writing on the signs
of shops. Many visitors find these charming 'little pictures' both new and somehow familiar. Some buy a
card with their own name written in Dongba to take home as a souvenir."
</details>

## Pictures and characters

Some Chinese characters began as pictures too: {山|shān}, {水|shuǐ}, {人|rén}, {日|rì}, {月|yuè} are the classic examples, and their
oldest forms, on bones and bronzes more than three thousand years old, look much like drawings.
But Chinese characters became a full writing system long ago, recording every word of the
language, and most characters today combine a meaning part and a sound part (like {情|qíng}, {请|qǐng}, {清|qīng}, {晴|qíng}, all
with {青|qīng} qīng). Dongba writing stayed much closer to pictures, and was kept by a small group of
specialists for a particular use. Looking at both side by side is a good way to see how much a
writing system can do, and how differently.

## Say it

```speak
# Lijiang
{丽江|Lì jiāng}{古城|gǔ chéng}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{百|bǎi}{年|nián}{的|de}{历史|lì shǐ}。
= The old town of Lijiang is several hundred years old.
{东巴文|Dōng bā wén}{很|hěn}{像|xiàng}{图画|tú huà}。
= Dongba writing looks like pictures.
{今天|jīn tiān}{能|néng}{读|dú}{懂|dǒng}{经书|jīng shū}{的|de}{东巴|dōng bā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{了|le}。
= Today very few dongba can still read the scriptures.
2003{年|nián}，{东巴|dōng bā}{古籍|gǔ jí}{被|bèi}{列入|liè rù}{了|le}《{世界记忆名录|Shì jiè Jì yì Míng lù}》。
= In 2003 the Dongba manuscripts were included in the Memory of the World Register.
```

## Words in this lesson

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {丽江|Lì jiāng} | Lijiang |
| {云南省|Yún nán shěng} | Yunnan province |
| {纳西族|Nà xī zú} | the Naxi |
| {东巴|dōng bā} | dongba (a Naxi ritual specialist) |
| {东巴文|Dōng bā wén} | the Dongba script |
| {哥巴文|Gē bā wén} | the Geba script |
| {象形文字|xiàng xíng wén zì} | pictographic writing |
| {古城|gǔ chéng} | old town |
| {铺|pū} | to pave |
| {宗教|zōng jiào} | religion |
| {仪式|yí shì} | ceremony (HSK 6) |
| {经书|jīng shū} | scriptures |
| {天文|tiān wén} | astronomy |
| {历法|lì fǎ} | calendar-making |
| {古籍|gǔ jí} | old books, ancient texts |
| {列入|liè rù} | to be included in (a list) |
| {联合国教科文组织|Lián hé guó Jiào kē wén zǔ zhī} | UNESCO |
| {世界文化遗产|shì jiè wén huà yí chǎn} | World (Cultural) Heritage Site |
| {世界记忆名录|Shì jiè Jì yì Míng lù} | the Memory of the World Register |
| {牌子|pái zi} | a sign, a board |
| {白沙|Bái shā} / {束河|Shù hé} | Baisha / Shuhe (villages near Lijiang) |

lessons.title: Study methods and training: how to improve
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about learning: how people study and train, how schools work, how we talk about
language, what science and technology change, and what we do online. This first lesson is about
getting better at something, at a desk or on a running track, and it ends with the task the HSK 5
standard gives for this topic: replying to an email about your own study methods.

You'll learn to:

- say what you judge something by: {从|cóng}{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{来|lái}{看|kàn} (judging from this match);
- describe trying again and again: {想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù} (after thinking it over and over), {走|zǒu}{来|lái}{走|zǒu}{去|qù} (walking up and down);
- say what helps, in a written way: {每|měi}{天|tiān}{复习|fù xí}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{记忆|jì yì} (reviewing every day helps memory);
- sum up with {总之|zǒng zhī} (in short), and talk about {分析|fēn xī} (analysing), {概括|gài kuò} (summarising) and {结论|jié lùn} (conclusions);
- use the words of study habits ({掌握|zhǎng wò}, {运用|yùn yòng}, {实践|shí jiàn}, {反复|fǎn fù}, {虚心|xū xīn}, {善于|shàn yú}…) and of training and contests
  ({训练|xùn liàn}, {选手|xuǎn shǒu}, {冠军|guàn jūn}, {决赛|jué sài}, {打破|dǎ pò}{纪录|jì lù}…).

## {从|cóng}…{来|lái}{看|kàn}: judging from…

{从|cóng} + a noun phrase + {来|lái}{看|kàn} introduces the evidence or the angle from which you judge. It's a
**[[viewpoint phrase]]**: it comes at the start, before the subject, and the rest of the sentence is
the judgment.

{从|cóng}{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，{他|tā}{的|de}{实力|shí lì}{还|hái}{不够|bú gòu}{强|qiáng}。 — Judging from this match, he isn't strong enough yet.

{从|cóng}{成绩|chéng jì}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，{这个|zhè ge}{办法|bàn fǎ}{很|hěn}{有效|yǒu xiào}。 — Judging by the results, this method works well.

{从|cóng}{长远|cháng yuǎn}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，{多|duō}{读书|dú shū}{对|duì}{写|xiě}{文章|wén zhāng}{很|hěn}{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù}。 — In the long run, reading a lot is a great help to your writing.

Two shorter forms say the same: {从|cóng}…{看|kàn} ({从|cóng}{他|tā}{的|de}{表情|biǎo qíng}{看|kàn}，{他|tā}{不|bú}{太|tài}{高兴|gāo xìng}, judging from his face, he isn't very
happy) and {从|cóng}…{上|shàng}{看|kàn}, used for an aspect ({从|cóng}{时间|shí jiān}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}, in terms of time). For "in my view", Chinese
uses a different frame, with a person: {在我看来|zài wǒ kàn lái} (in my view). Compare:

| Frame | What follows it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {从|cóng} + evidence + {来|lái}{看|kàn} | a judgment drawn from the evidence | {从|cóng}{他|tā}{的|de}{成绩|chéng jì}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，{他|tā}{很|hěn}{努力|nǔ lì}。 Judging by his marks, he works hard. |
| {从|cóng} + aspect + {上|shàng}{看|kàn} | how things look in that respect | {从|cóng}{时间|shí jiān}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}，{坐|zuò}{高铁|gāo tiě}{更|gèng}{方便|fāng biàn}。 In terms of time, the high-speed train is more convenient. |
| {在|zài} + person + {看来|kàn lái} | that person's opinion | {在我看来|zài wǒ kàn lái}，{方法|fāng fǎ}{比|bǐ}{时间|shí jiān}{更|gèng}{重要|zhòng yào}。 In my view, method matters more than time. |

Don't drop {从|cóng}: ~~{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{来|lái}{看|kàn}~~ has no frame. And {来|lái}{看|kàn} is two words here, {来|lái} + {看|kàn}, not the verb
"to come and see": the sentence is not about anyone coming.

## A{来|lái}A{去|qù}: over and over, back and forth

A verb repeated with {来|lái} and {去|qù} is one of the **[[four-character patterns]]** of HSK 5: the action is done
again and again, or back and forth.

{他|tā}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{走|zǒu}{来|lái}{走|zǒu}{去|qù}。 — He was walking up and down outside the door.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{钥匙|yào shi}{找|zhǎo}{来|lái}{找|zhǎo}{去|qù}{也|yě}{没|méi}{找|zhǎo}{到|dào}。 — I looked everywhere for my keys and still didn't find them.

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{还是|hái shi}{决定|jué dìng}{先|xiān}{不|bú}{报名|bào míng}。 — I thought it over and over, and in the end I decided not to sign up for now.

The pattern usually needs a second clause saying how it turned out, often with {还是|hái shi} (in the end, after
all) or {也|yě} (even so). {说|shuō}{来|lái}{说|shuō}{去|qù} has a set meaning of its own: "whichever way you put it, it comes down
to…": {说|shuō}{来|lái}{说|shuō}{去|qù}，{还是|hái shi}{方法|fāng fǎ}{的|de}{问题|wèn tí} (all said and done, it's a question of method). The pattern takes
one-syllable verbs: {想|xiǎng}, {走|zǒu}, {找|zhǎo}, {说|shuō}, {看|kàn}, {练|liàn}, {改|gǎi}. Lesson 10 had another four-character pattern, {说|shuō}A{就|jiù}A
({说|shuō}{走|zǒu}{就|jiù}{走|zǒu}, off at a moment's notice); there are more in this module's reference sheet.

## {有助于|yǒu zhù yú}: helps, is good for (written)

{有助于|yǒu zhù yú} is {有|yǒu} + {助|zhù} (help) + {于|yú} (to, for: HSK 4's written {于|yú}), so the thing it helps follows it
directly:

{每|měi}{天|tiān}{复习|fù xí}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{记忆|jì yì}。 — Reviewing every day helps you remember.

{适当|shì dàng}{的|de}{运动|yùn dòng}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{睡眠|shuì mián}。 — The right amount of exercise is good for sleep.

{多|duō}{跟|gēn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{聊天|liáo tiān}，{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{提高|tí gāo}{口语|kǒu yǔ}。 — Chatting with Chinese people a lot helps improve your speaking.

In speech, people more often say {对|duì}…{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù} or {对|duì}…{有|yǒu}{好处|hǎo chù}: {每|měi}{天|tiān}{复习|fù xí}{对|duì}{记忆|jì yì}{很|hěn}{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù}. Both are correct;
{有助于|yǒu zhù yú} belongs in writing (reports, essays, advice columns). Two mistakes: {有助于|yǒu zhù yú} takes no {很|hěn} (×{很|hěn}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}),
and the thing helped can't come before it with {对|duì}: ~~{对|duì}{记忆|jì yì}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}~~ leaves {于|yú} with nothing after it.
Write {有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{记忆|jì yì}, or {对|duì}{记忆|jì yì}{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù}.

## {总之|zǒng zhī}: in short

{总之|zǒng zhī} sums up after several points, at the start of the last sentence:

{多|duō}{听|tīng}、{多|duō}{说|shuō}、{多|duō}{读|dú}、{多|duō}{写|xiě}，{总之|zǒng zhī}，{要|yào}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{用|yòng}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Listen a lot, speak a lot, read a lot, write a lot: in short,
use Chinese every day.

It can also cut a discussion short, like "anyway, at any rate": {总之|zǒng zhī}，{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{担心|dān xīn}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{准时|zhǔn shí}{到|dào}{的|de} (anyway,
don't worry, I'll be there on time). {总之|zǒng zhī} is fine in speech and writing. Two near neighbours: {总的来说|zǒng de lái shuō}
(on the whole, generally speaking: {总的来说|zǒng de lái shuō}，{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{很|hěn}{成功|chéng gōng}) and {反正|fǎn zhèng} (lesson 06: anyway, whatever happens),
which isn't a summary at all.

## Analysing, summarising, concluding

Three words for thinking about what you've done:

- {分析|fēn xī} (to analyse; analysis): {分析|fēn xī}{原因|yuán yīn} (analyse the reasons), {分析|fēn xī}{问题|wèn tí}, {分析|fēn xī}{比赛|bǐ sài}. {他|tā}{的|de}{分析|fēn xī}{很|hěn}{有|yǒu}{道理|dào li} (his
  analysis makes a lot of sense; {道理|dào li}, sense, is lesson 26's word).
- {概括|gài kuò} (to summarise; a summary): {请|qǐng}{概括|gài kuò}{一下|yí xià}{这|zhè}{篇|piān}{文章|wén zhāng}{的|de}{主要|zhǔ yào}{内容|nèi róng} (please sum up the main content of this
  article). An exam favourite: "{用|yòng}{一|yí}{句|jù}{话|huà}{概括|gài kuò}…".
- {结论|jié lùn} (a conclusion): {得出|dé chū}{结论|jié lùn} (to reach a conclusion; {得出|dé chū} dé chū), {下结论|xià jié lùn} (to draw a conclusion):
  {现在|xiàn zài}{下结论|xià jié lùn}{还|hái}{太|tài}{早|zǎo} (it's too early to draw conclusions).

Put them together and you have the shape of an argued paragraph: {先|xiān}{分析|fēn xī}，{再|zài}{概括|gài kuò}，{最后|zuì hòu}{得出|dé chū}{结论|jié lùn}.

## Words for studying well

Many of this lesson's words come in fixed pairs. Learn them with their partners.

| Word | Meaning | With its partner |
|---|---|---|
| {掌握|zhǎng wò} | to master, grasp | {掌握|zhǎng wò}{技能|jì néng} (master a skill), {掌握|zhǎng wò}{方法|fāng fǎ} |
| {熟练|shú liàn} | skilled, fluent | {熟练|shú liàn}{地|de}{使用|shǐ yòng}{电脑|diàn nǎo} (use a computer with ease) |
| {运用|yùn yòng} | to use, apply | {灵活|líng huó}{运用|yùn yòng} (use flexibly), {运用|yùn yòng}{学|xué}{到|dào}{的|de}{知识|zhī shi} |
| {实践|shí jiàn} | practice; to put into practice | {在|zài}{实践|shí jiàn}{中|zhōng}{学习|xué xí} (learn by doing) |
| {体会|tǐ huì} | to come to understand; what you understand from experience | {我|wǒ}{体会|tǐ huì}{到|dào}{了|le}{坚持|jiān chí}{的|de}{重要|zhòng yào} |
| {思考|sī kǎo} / {思维|sī wéi} | to think hard, ponder / way of thinking | {善于|shàn yú}{思考|sī kǎo}; {他|tā}{的|de}{思维|sī wéi}{很|hěn}{灵活|líng huó} |
| {记忆|jì yì} | memory; to remember | {记忆|jì yì}{力|lì} (memory, the ability); {加深|jiā shēn}{记忆|jì yì} |
| {记录|jì lù} | to record, take notes; notes | {把|bǎ}{问题|wèn tí}{记录|jì lù}{下来|xià lái} (write the problems down) |
| {观察|guān chá} | to observe | {仔细|zǐ xì}{观察|guān chá} (observe closely) |

**A new radical: 冖 (the cover).** 冖 is a flat lid: a dot, then a horizontal stroke that hooks
down at its end. Its common name is {秃宝盖|tū bǎo gài}, a "bald" 宀 (the roof of {家|jiā}) without its top dot. You've
met it in {写|xiě} and {农|nóng}, and now in {冠|guàn}, where it sits over {元|yuán} and {寸|cùn}. In {军|jūn} it sits on top too; some

  sound part of 晰 xī ({清晰|qīng xī}, clear, HSK 6). {佳|jiā} is 亻 + 圭, the same 圭 as in the middle of {街|jiē} jiē
  and on the right of {鞋|xié} xié, where the sound has drifted. {荐|jiàn} is 艹 over {存|cún}.
- **{录|lù} and {灵|líng}** both have 彐 on top, the third character with it after {寻|xún} ({寻找|xún zhǎo}, lesson 11): it's the
  new radical of lesson 12. Under it, {录|lù} has 氺 (a form of {水|shuǐ}) and {灵|líng} has {火|huǒ} (fire).

  ({实践|shí jiàn}) a plan on foot.

### Stroke order

- **{军|jūn}** (6): 冖 (dot, horizontal hook), then 车: horizontal, the turning stroke, horizontal,
  and the long vertical last.
- **{录|lù}** (8): 彐 (horizontal-turn, horizontal, horizontal), then the vertical hook, the dot and the
  rising stroke on the left, and the left-falling and right-falling strokes on the right.
- **{胜|shèng}** (9): ⺼ first (left-falling, horizontal-turn-hook, two short horizontals), then {生|shēng}
  (left-falling, horizontal, horizontal, vertical, and the long bottom horizontal).
- **{抓|zhuā}** (7): 扌 (horizontal, vertical hook, rising stroke), then 爪 (left-falling, a vertical
  left-falling stroke, vertical, right-falling).
- **{析|xī}** (8): {木|mù} with its last stroke shortened to a dot (horizontal, vertical, left-falling, dot),
  then {斤|jīn} (left-falling, left-falling, horizontal, vertical).
- **{冠|guàn}** (9): 冖 first; then {元|yuán} (horizontal, horizontal, left-falling, the vertical-bend-hook);
  then {寸|cùn} (horizontal, vertical hook, dot).

You ask how I learned English and whether I have any good methods. To tell the truth, my methods
aren't anything special, but I have learned a few things these two years, so here they are in brief.

bed I go over the words I learned that day. An hour every day works much better than seven hours in
one go at the weekend. In my experience, learning a language is like training for a sport: what

exchange every week and chatted with British students. At first I was very nervous and often got
things wrong, but gradually I stopped being afraid. As for vocabulary, what I've found is this: don't learn words one by one, put them into sentences. not to make the same mistake twice. Also, when you don't understand something, ask, and be open to
advice. I often ask British students to correct my essays, and their comments help me a lot.

## Pronunciation

- {纪录|jì lù} and {记录|jì lù} are both jì lù: only the characters tell them apart.
- {冠军|guàn jūn} guàn jūn: {冠|guàn} is fourth tone here ("first place"). Read guān (first tone) it is a crown or a
  hat, in words you'll meet later.
- {综合|zōng hé} zōng hé (not zòng); {思维|sī wéi} sī wéi; {把握|bǎ wò} bǎ wò (3+4).
- {熟练|shú liàn} shú liàn: {熟|shú} is also heard shóu in everyday speech in the north; shú is the standard reading.
- {请教|qǐng jiào} qǐng jiào: {教|jiào} is jiào here, as in {教室|jiào shì} and {教练|jiào liàn}, not the {教|jiāo} jiāo of "to teach (someone something)".
- {想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù} xiǎng lái xiǎng qù: {来|lái} and {去|qù} are said lightly in the pattern, but they keep their tones.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，{他|tā}{不够|bú gòu}{强|qiáng}~~: the frame needs {从|cóng}: {从|cóng}{这|zhè}{次|cì}{比赛|bǐ sài}{来|lái}{看|kàn}，….
- ~~{对|duì}{记忆|jì yì}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}~~ and ~~{很|hěn}{有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{记忆|jì yì}~~: {有助于|yǒu zhù yú} takes what it helps straight after it, and no {很|hěn}: {有助于|yǒu zhù yú}{记忆|jì yì}
  (or {对|duì}{记忆|jì yì}{很|hěn}{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù}).
- ~~{他|tā}{打破|dǎ pò}{了|le}{记录|jì lù}~~: a best result is {纪录|jì lù} (with {=纟=}); {记录|jì lù} (with {=讠=}) is notes, minutes, writing down.
- ~~{修改|xiū gǎi}{错误|cuò wù}~~ for "correct a mistake": less natural; mistakes are {改正|gǎi zhèng} ({改正|gǎi zhèng}{错误|cuò wù}). {修改|xiū gǎi} is for improving a
  text or a plan.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{想|xiǎng}{来|lái}~~: the order is fixed: {来|lái} first, then {去|qù} ({想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}).

## Key points

- {从|cóng} + evidence or aspect + {来|lái}{看|kàn} / {看|kàn} / {上|shàng}{看|kàn}: judging from…; {在|zài} + person + {看来|kàn lái}: in someone's view.
- A{来|lái}A{去|qù} ({想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}, {找|zhǎo}{来|lái}{找|zhǎo}{去|qù}, {走|zǒu}{来|lái}{走|zǒu}{去|qù}): again and again, back and forth; a second clause says how it ended.
  {说|shuō}{来|lái}{说|shuō}{去|qù}: all said and done.
- {有助于|yǒu zhù yú} + what it helps (written); in speech {对|duì}…{有|yǒu}{帮助|bāng zhù} / {有|yǒu}{好处|hǎo chù}.
- {总之|zǒng zhī}: in short, at any rate. {总的来说|zǒng de lái shuō}: on the whole. {分析|fēn xī}, {概括|gài kuò}, {得出|dé chū} / {下结论|xià jié lùn}.
- {纪录|jì lù} (a record) vs {记录|jì lù} (to note down); {修改|xiū gǎi} (improve) vs {改正|gǎi zhèng} (correct); {胜|shèng} (written) vs {赢|yíng}.
- Reply to an email in points, with examples and connectors, and sum up with {总之|zǒng zhī}.
- New characters: {裁|cái} {析|xī}✎ {冠|guàn} {军|jūn}✎ {录|lù}✎ {灵|líng} {胜|shèng}✎ {践|jiàn} {荐|jiàn} {虚|xū} {抓|zhuā}✎ {综|zōng} {佳|jiā}; new radical {=冖=}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Schools, universities and exams
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 was about how to learn; this one is about where. You'll follow a Chinese student from
{幼儿园|yòu ér yuán} (kindergarten) to university, sit in on a meeting about {安娜|Ān nà}'s (Anna's) thesis plan with
{罗|Luó}{教授|jiào shòu} (Professor Luo), and learn to:

- say how often things happen, from {通常|tōng cháng} (usually) and {时常|shí cháng} (often, written) to HSK 4's {往往|wǎng wǎng} and {经常|jīng cháng};
- describe gradual change with {渐渐|jiàn jiàn} (gradually);
- count schools with {所|suǒ} ({一|yì}{所|suǒ}{大学|dà xué}) and sessions and graduating years with {届|jiè} ({第|dì}{十|shí}{届|jiè}, 2030{届|jiè});
- use three words that look like old friends but aren't: {={系|xì}=} xì (a department), {数|shǔ} shǔ (to count) and
  {才|cái} cái (talent);
- name school subjects, university life and exams ({学科|xué kē}, {学分|xué fēn}, {论文|lùn wén}, {试卷|shì juàn}, {及格|jí gé}, {录取|lù qǔ}…).

The module's speaking task, retelling a passage, comes near the end.

## {通常|tōng cháng}, {时常|shí cháng}, {往往|wǎng wǎng}, {经常|jīng cháng}: how often

Four words, four jobs:

| Word | Meaning | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {通常|tōng cháng} | usually, as a rule | what normally happens; can start the sentence; also "usual" before a noun | {我|wǒ}{通常|tōng cháng}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。{通常|tōng cháng}{情况|qíng kuàng}{下|xià}，{考试|kǎo shì}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}。 |
| {经常|jīng cháng} / {常常|cháng cháng} | often | the everyday word | {他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}。 |
| {时常|shí cháng} | often | written, a little formal | {老师|lǎo shī}{时常|shí cháng}{提醒|tí xǐng}{我们|wǒ men}{注意|zhù yì}{时间|shí jiān}。 |
| {往往|wǎng wǎng} | tends to, is apt to | what tends to happen when a condition is met: needs that condition | {考试|kǎo shì}{前|qián}{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{学生|xué sheng}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{睡|shuì}{得|de}{很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}。 |

{通常|tōng cháng} is about the normal case, so it often comes with a contrast: {我|wǒ}{通常|tōng cháng}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{上班|shàng bān}，{今天|jīn tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{就|jiù}{打车|dǎ chē}{了|le}
(I usually take the metro, but today it rained, so I took a taxi). Before a noun it means "usual,
normal": {通常|tōng cháng}{的|de}{做法|zuò fǎ} (the usual way of doing it).

{往往|wǎng wǎng} needs a pattern you've observed, and it can't be used for plans or the future: ~~{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}
{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}~~ is wrong; say {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}, or {我|wǒ}{经常|jīng cháng}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}. Nor can it describe one person's single
habit without a condition: {他|tā}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn} sounds incomplete, while {一|yì}{有|yǒu}{空|kòng}，{他|tā}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{就|jiù}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn} (whenever he has
a moment, he tends to go to the library) is fine.

## {渐渐|jiàn jiàn}: gradually

{渐渐|jiàn jiàn} (often {渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{地|de}) describes change that happens little by little, by itself:

{天|tiān}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{冷|lěng}{了|le}。 — It was gradually getting colder.

{刚|gāng}{来|lái}{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{习惯|xí guàn}{这里|zhè lǐ}{的|de}{冬天|dōng tiān}，{后来|hòu lái}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{习惯|xí guàn}{了|le}。 — When I first came to Beijing I wasn't used to the
winters here; later I gradually got used to them.

{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{地|de}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{对|duì}{这|zhè}{门|mén}{课|kè}{有|yǒu}{了|le}{兴趣|xìng qù}。 — Gradually, everyone took an interest in the subject.

{渐渐|jiàn jiàn} is about change, not speed: it can't ask someone to do something slowly. ~~{请|qǐng}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{说|shuō}~~ is wrong;
"please speak slowly" is {请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{说|shuō}. Its neighbours: {慢|màn}{慢|màn} (spoken: {慢|màn}{慢|màn}{就|jiù}{习惯|xí guàn}{了|le}, you'll get used to it in time)
and {逐渐|zhú jiàn} (lesson 22: more written, for planned or steady change).

## Counting schools and sessions: {所|suǒ} and {届|jiè}

{所|suǒ} counts institutions with buildings, above all schools and hospitals:

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{一|yì}{所|suǒ}{很|hěn}{有名|yǒu míng}{的|de}{大学|dà xué}。 — This is a well-known university.

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{附近|fù jìn}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{所|suǒ}{小学|xiǎo xué}{和|hé}{一|yì}{所|suǒ}{医院|yī yuàn}。 — Near my home there are two primary schools and a hospital.

Companies, shops and restaurants take {家|jiā} ({一|yì}{家|jiā}{公司|gōng sī}, {一|yì}{家|jiā}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}); a school can take {家|jiā} in speech too,
but {所|suǒ} is the usual written choice.

{届|jiè} counts the sessions of a regular event and the year-groups of graduates:

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{第|dì}{十|shí}{届|jiè}{学生|xué sheng}{运动会|yùn dòng huì}。 — This is the tenth students' sports meeting.

{她|tā}{是|shì}2030{届|jiè}{的|de}{毕业生|bì yè shēng}。 — She graduates in 2030 (she's in the class of 2030).

{本|běn}{届|jiè} is "this session" (written), {上|shàng}{一|yí}{届|jiè} "the last one" and {下|xià}{一|yí}{届|jiè} "the next one": {下|xià}{一|yí}{届|jiè}{比赛|bǐ sài}{在|zài}{明年|míng nián}{举行|jǔ xíng}.

## Three new readings: {={系|xì}=} xì, {数|shǔ} shǔ, {才|cái} cái

**{={系|xì}=} xì: a department.** A university has {学院|xué yuàn} (colleges, HSK 4), which have {={系|xì}=} (departments), in
which students take a {专业|zhuān yè} (a major): {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{中文|Zhōng wén}{系|xì}{的|de}{学生|xué sheng} (I'm a student in the Chinese department), {物理|wù lǐ}{系|xì},
{系|xì}{主任|zhǔ rèn} (the head of department). You know {={系|xì}=} from {关系|guān xi} and {联系|lián xì}; lesson 15's {={系|jì}=} jì is "to tie" (a
ribbon). With the traditional script on, the department stays {={系|xì}=} and "to tie" becomes 繫.

**{数|shǔ} shǔ: to count.** HSK 4's {数|shù} shù is a number ({数字|shù zì}, {数学|shù xué}). Read shǔ, third tone, it's the verb:

{你|nǐ}{数一数|shǔ yi shǔ}，{一共|yí gòng}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{本|běn}{书|shū}？ — Count them: how many books are there?

{作业|zuò yè}{多|duō}{得|de}{数|shǔ}{不|bu}{清|qīng}。 — There's more homework than you could count.

{数|shǔ}{不|bu}{清|qīng} (too many to count) is the potential complement. A set phrase: {数一数二|shǔ yī shǔ èr} (one of the very best,
literally "counted first or second").

**{才|cái} cái: talent.** HSK 3's {才|cái} is the adverb "only then, not until". As a noun it's talent, ability,
as in lesson 01's {人才|rén cái} (talented people): {他|tā}{很|hěn}{有才|yǒu cái} (he's very talented). The traditional script keeps
{才|cái} for both.

## Words for school and university

**From kindergarten to university.** {幼儿园|yòu ér yuán} (kindergarten), then {小学|xiǎo xué} and {中学|zhōng xué} (HSK 1), {初中|chū zhōng} and {高中|gāo zhōng}, and the
university. Subjects: {语文|yǔ wén} (Chinese, the school subject), {数学|shù xué}, {历史|lì shǐ}, {地理|dì lǐ} (geography), {物理|wù lǐ} (physics), {化学|huà xué}
(chemistry), {生物|shēng wù} (biology, lesson 19), {政治|zhèng zhì} (politics, as a school subject), {哲学|zhé xué} (philosophy). {学科|xué kē} is a
subject or discipline in general: {这|zhè}{所|suǒ}{大学|dà xué}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{学科|xué kē}.

**Exams.** {试卷|shì juàn} (an exam paper), {题目|tí mù} (a question on it; also a topic, a title), {填|tián} (to fill in: {填空|tián kòng}, fill
the gaps; {填表|tián biǎo}, fill in a form), {难度|nán dù} (difficulty: {难度|nán dù}{很|hěn}{大|dà}), {及格|jí gé} (to pass: {六十|liù shí}{分|fēn}{及格|jí gé}), {录取|lù qǔ} (to admit: {他|tā}{被|bèi}{这|zhè}{所|suǒ}{大学|dà xué}
{录取|lù qǔ}{了|le}), and the levels {初级|chū jí} / {中级|zhōng jí} / {高级|gāo jí} (elementary / intermediate / advanced) of a {级|jí} (a level, a grade:
{这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}{是|shì}{中级|zhōng jí}{的|de}).

**University life.** {学年|xué nián} (an academic year), {学分|xué fēn} (a credit: {这|zhè}{门|mén}{课|kè}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{学分|xué fēn}), {宿舍|sù shè} (a dormitory), {讲座|jiǎng zuò} (a lecture,
usually a one-off talk: {听|tīng}{讲座|jiǎng zuò}), {论文|lùn wén} (a thesis, a paper), {教材|jiào cái} (a textbook, teaching materials), {图书|tú shū} (books, in
general: {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} is HSK 3's library), {学术|xué shù} (academic: {学术|xué shù}{讲座|jiǎng zuò}, {学术|xué shù}{论文|lùn wén}), {学者|xué zhě} (a scholar), {提交|tí jiāo} (to submit:
{提交|tí jiāo}{论文|lùn wén}). Things in a pencil case: {尺子|chǐ zi} (a ruler) and {橡皮|xiàng pí} (an eraser); in the corridor, the {铃|líng} (a bell:
{上课|shàng kè}{铃|líng}{响|xiǎng}{了|le}).

**Teaching and growing.** {培养|péi yǎng} (to cultivate, to train: {培养|péi yǎng}{人才|rén cái}, {培养|péi yǎng}{兴趣|xìng qù}), {指导|zhǐ dǎo} (to guide, to supervise:
{指导|zhǐ dǎo}{老师|lǎo shī}, a supervisor), {评|píng} (to judge, assess: {评一评|píng yi píng}, {评|píng}{上|shàng}{了|le} (was chosen as)), {改革|gǎi gé} (to reform; a reform), {勤奋|qín fèn}
(diligent, hard-working), {本领|běn lǐng} (skill, ability: {学|xué}{本领|běn lǐng}), {常识|cháng shí} (common knowledge: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{常识|cháng shí}), {理论|lǐ lùn} (a theory:
{理论|lǐ lùn}{和|hé}{实践|shí jiàn}), {观念|guān niàn} (an idea, a concept: {老|lǎo}{观念|guān niàn}, old ways of thinking), {思想|sī xiǎng} (thought, ideas), {向上|xiàng shàng} (upward:
{好好|hǎo hǎo}{学习|xué xí}，{天|tiān}{天|tiān}{向上|xiàng shàng}, a well-known school slogan: "study well and make progress every day").

{学者|xué zhě} is a scholar; HSK 4's {学生|xué sheng} a student, and {读者|dú zhě} a reader: {者|zhě} is the suffix "a person who".

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Traditional | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 尺 ✎ | ruler; the chi (a third of a metre) | chǐ | 尸 | 4 | 尺 | {尺子|chǐ zi} |
| 革 | leather; change | gé | 革 | 9 | 革 | {改革|gǎi gé} |
| 渐 | gradually | jiàn | 氵 | 11 | 漸 | {渐渐|jiàn jiàn} |
| 铃 | bell | líng | 钅 | 10 | 鈴 | {铃|líng} |
| 届 | session; year (of graduates) | jiè | 尸 | 8 | 屆 | {届|jiè} |
| 勤 | diligent | qín | 力 | 13 | 勤 | {勤奋|qín fèn} |
| 卷 | paper, scroll | juàn | 㔾 | 8 | 卷 | {试卷|shì juàn} |
| 宿 ✎ | stay overnight | sù | 宀 | 11 | 宿 | {宿舍|sù shè} |
| 橡 | rubber tree | xiàng | 木 | 15 | 橡 | {橡皮|xiàng pí} |
| 幼 | young | yòu | 幺 | 5 | 幼 | {幼儿园|yòu ér yuán} |
| 哲 | wise | zhé | 口 | 10 | 哲 | {哲学|zhé xué} |
| 政 ✎ | government, politics | zhèng | 攵 | 9 | 政 | {政治|zhèng zhì} |

Only three change in traditional: 漸 (14 strokes, with 斬 on the right), 鈴 (13, with 金 on the
left) and 屆 (8, with another part under 尸 where simplified has {由|yóu}). In {试卷|shì juàn} and {问卷|wèn juàn} the
traditional form is {卷|juàn} too: 捲 is a different character, "to roll up".

**A new radical: 幺 (tiny).** 幺 yāo is something small and thin, a twist of thread. It's in {乡|xiāng}
({家乡|jiā xiāng}, HSK 4), in {幽默|yōu mò}'s {幽|yōu}, and now in {幼|yòu} (young: 幺 + {力|lì}). The reading yāo of {一|yāo} in phone numbers
is the same syllable.

- **Sound parts.** {政|zhèng} is {正|zhèng} zhèng + 攵: the sound is exact. {哲|zhé} is {折|zhé} zhé ({打折|dǎ zhé}, HSK 4) over {口|kǒu}: exact again.
  {橡|xiàng} is {木|mù} + {象|xiàng} xiàng ({印象|yìn xiàng}, HSK 4): exact. {铃|líng} is 钅 (metal) + {令|lìng}: {令|lìng} lìng gives the sound of a whole
  family, all near ling: {零|líng} líng (zero), {龄|líng} líng ({年龄|nián líng}), {铃|líng} líng, {领|lǐng} lǐng ({领导|lǐng dǎo}, lesson 02), {冷|lěng} lěng.
- **A meaning part.** {革|gé} is leather; it's on the left of {鞋|xié} (shoe). {勤|qín} has {力|lì} (strength, effort) on the
  right, like {劝|quàn} (and at the bottom of {努|nǔ}).
- **尸 again.** {尺|chǐ} and {届|jiè} both sit under 尸, the same top as {层|céng} and {局|jú}. In {尺|chǐ}, under it, is a long
  right-falling stroke; in {届|jiè} it's {由|yóu}.
- **{宿|sù}** is 宀 (a roof) over 亻 and {百|bǎi}. {宿舍|sù shè} sù shè: both characters are about a place to stay.
- **Look-alikes**: {幼|yòu} yòu and {幻|huàn} huàn (HSK 6) differ on the right ({力|lì} and a hook); {卷|juàn} juàn and {券|quàn} quàn
  (a ticket, as in {优惠券|yōu huì quàn}, a coupon) share the top, with 㔾 or {刀|dāo} below.

### Stroke order

- **{尺|chǐ}** (4): horizontal-turn, horizontal, left-falling, then the long right-falling stroke.
- **{宿|sù}** (11): 宀 (dot, dot, horizontal hook), then 亻, then {百|bǎi} (horizontal, left-falling, then {日|rì}).
- **{政|zhèng}** (9): {正|zhèng} (horizontal, vertical, horizontal, vertical, and a rising stroke at the bottom, not a
  horizontal), then 攵 (left-falling, horizontal, left-falling, right-falling).
- **{幼|yòu}** (5): 幺 (two turning strokes and a dot), then {力|lì} (horizontal-turn-hook, left-falling).
- **{届|jiè}** (8): 尸 (horizontal-turn, horizontal, left-falling), then {由|yóu}.

```trace
尺革渐铃届勤
```

```trace
卷宿橡幼哲政
```

**Write it**: {尺|chǐ} {宿|sù} {政|zhèng} are handwriting characters (✎). Write each three times from memory, then {尺子|chǐ zi},
{宿舍|sù shè}, {政治|zhèng zhì}.
=}

## Dialogue: a thesis that's too big

{安娜|Ān nà} is in her final year. In lesson 10h1 she told {罗|Luó}{教授|jiào shòu}, her supervisor, what interested her
(Jingdezhen blue-and-white, and how porcelain reached Europe); the written plan she brings him now tries to
cover the whole history of porcelain.

```dialogue
# The thesis plan
安娜: {罗|Luó}{教授|jiào shòu}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{论文|lùn wén}{计划|jì huà}，{请|qǐng}{您|nín}{指导|zhǐ dǎo}{一下|yí xià}。
= Hello, Professor Luo! This is my thesis plan. Could you give me some guidance?
罗教授: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{先|xiān}{看看|kàn kan}。{题目|tí mù}{是|shì}《{中国|Zhōng guó}{瓷器|cí qì}{的|de}{历史|lì shǐ}》？{这个|zhè ge}{题目|tí mù}{太|tài}{大|dà}{了|le}。
= Right, let me have a look. The title is "The History of Chinese Porcelain"? That's far too big a topic.
安娜: {太|tài}{大|dà}{了|le}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{瓷器|cí qì}{很|hěn}{有意思|yǒu yì si}，{想|xiǎng}{全面|quán miàn}{地|de}{写一写|xiě yi xiě}。
= Too big? I find porcelain fascinating, and I wanted to cover it all.
罗教授: {本科|běn kē}{论文|lùn wén}{通常|tōng cháng}{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{一万|yí wàn}{字|zì}{左右|zuǒ yòu}。{这么|zhè me}{大|dà}{的|de}{题目|tí mù}，{写|xiě}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}{都|dōu}{不够|bú gòu}。{你|nǐ}{最|zuì}{感兴趣|gǎn xìng qù}{的|de}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{一|yí}{部分|bù fen}？
= An undergraduate thesis is usually only about ten thousand characters. A topic like this wouldn't fit in a whole book. Which part interests you most?
```

1. Her path through school, from kindergarten to university, and what each stage gave her.
2. Her teacher didn't criticise her but helped her after class and taught her how to analyse

"**From kindergarten to university**, by Fang Qing. I started kindergarten at three. The best
thing every day then was listening to the teacher tell stories and learning songs. The year I was
six, I went to a primary school next to my home. There weren't many lessons in primary school:
mainly Chinese and maths. Every day after school I often played on the sports ground with my
classmates, and only ran back to the classroom when I heard the bell. In junior high, the subjects
suddenly multiplied: physics, chemistry, geography, history, politics… and they got harder and
harder. I wasn't very good at physics, and I nearly failed my first test. My physics teacher didn't
criticise me; instead he patiently helped me after class and taught me how to analyse the questions.
Gradually my marks went up, and I became interested in physics. The three years of senior high were
the busiest. We lived in the school dormitory, got up at six and didn't go to bed until ten. There
were tests every week and more exam papers than you could count. Everybody knows that your {高考|gāo kǎo} result
decides which university will admit you, so nobody dared to relax. When I went home at weekends, my mum always cooked a whole table of good food: those were the most relaxed hours of my week. Last summer I was admitted to
the physics department of a university. University is completely different from high school: the
teachers don't check your homework every day, and studying depends on your own initiative. In one
academic year you take over forty credits. As well as classes, you can go to all kinds of academic
lectures. Last month I heard a lecture by a famous scholar. He said: 'University doesn't just give
you skills; more importantly, it trains your ability to think.' I've kept that sentence in mind ever
since. The teachers in our department often get us to ask questions and discuss in class. At first I
wasn't used to it at all, because in secondary school we usually just listened and took notes. Now
I'm gradually coming to see that asking a good question is more useful than remembering an answer. Looking back on these ten-odd years, what I've learned most of all is that every stretch of
the road is hard, but every stretch has given me something."

{考试|kǎo shì}{那|nà}{天|tiān}，{小|Xiǎo}{王|Wáng}{起|qǐ}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}。{他|tā}{跑|pǎo}{进|jìn}{考场|kǎo chǎng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{铃|líng}{声|shēng}{正好|zhèng hǎo}{响|xiǎng}{了|le}。{他|tā}{坐|zuò}{下来|xià lái}{打开|dǎ kāi}{笔袋|bǐ dài}，{发现|fā xiàn}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{带|dài}{橡皮|xiàng pí}。{他|tā}{正|zhèng}{着急|zháo jí}，{旁边|páng biān}{的|de}{女|nǚ}{同学|tóng xué}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}，{用|yòng}{尺子|chǐ zi}{把|bǎ}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{橡皮|xiàng pí}{切|qiē}{成|chéng}{两半|liǎng bàn}，{给|gěi}{了|le}{他|tā}{一半|yí bàn}。{考试|kǎo shì}{结束|jié shù}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{小|Xiǎo}{王|Wáng}{对|duì}{她|tā}{说|shuō}：“{太|tài}{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}{了|le}！{没有|méi yǒu}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{半|bàn}{块|kuài}{橡皮|xiàng pí}，{我|wǒ}{真|zhēn}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{怎么办|zěn me bàn}。”{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{一边|yì biān}{说|shuō}{一边|yì biān}{笑|xiào}{着|zhe}{走|zǒu}{出|chū}{了|le}{考场|kǎo chǎng}。

({考场|kǎo chǎng}: the exam room; {笔袋|bǐ dài}: a pencil case; {两半|liǎng bàn}: two halves.)
</details>

## Write it: a teacher who made a difference

Write 200–300 characters on a teacher who changed the way you study. Plan: who and when; what
the problem was; what the teacher did (one scene in detail); what changed ({渐渐|jiàn jiàn}…); what you
learned ({一|yí}{句|jù}{话|huà}{概括|gài kuò}).

<details>
<summary>Model essay</summary>

{我|wǒ}{上|shàng}{初中|chū zhōng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{最|zuì}{怕|pà}{的|de}{课|kè}{是|shì}{数学|shù xué}。{每|měi}{次|cì}{考试|kǎo shì}，{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{刚刚|gāng gāng}{及格|jí gé}，{我|wǒ}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{觉得|jué de}{自己|zì jǐ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{学|xué}{数学|shù xué}{的|de}{人|rén}。

{初二|chū èr}{那|nà}{年|nián}，{我们|wǒ men}{来|lái}{了|le}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{新|xīn}{的|de}{数学|shù xué}{老师|lǎo shī}。{她|tā}{发现|fā xiàn}{我|wǒ}{做|zuò}{题|tí}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{只|zhǐ}{记|jì}{公式|gōng shì}，{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{为什么|wèi shén me}。{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{天|tiān}{放学|fàng xué}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{她|tā}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{留|liú}{下来|xià lái}，{不|bù}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{讲|jiǎng}{答案|dá àn}，{而|ér}{是|shì}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{题目|tí mù}{读|dú}{三|sān}{遍|biàn}，{再|zài}{用|yòng}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{话|huà}{说|shuō}{出|chū}{题目|tí mù}{问|wèn}{的|de}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}。{开始|kāi shǐ}{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{这个|zhè ge}{办法|bàn fǎ}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}，{可是|kě shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{月|yuè}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{我|wǒ}{发现|fā xiàn}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{题目|tí mù}{一|yì}{读|dú}{懂|dǒng}，{就|jiù}{知道|zhī dào}{怎么|zěn me}{做|zuò}{了|le}。

{那个|nà ge}{学期|xué qī}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{数学|shù xué}{从|cóng}{六十|liù shí}{多|duō}{分|fēn}{提高|tí gāo}{到|dào}{了|le}{八十|bā shí}{多|duō}{分|fēn}。{更|gèng}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{再|zài}{怕|pà}{数学|shù xué}{了|le}。{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{也|yě}{用|yòng}{她|tā}{的|de}{方法|fāng fǎ}：{先|xiān}{弄|nòng}{懂|dǒng}，{再|zài}{记|jì}{住|zhù}。{用|yòng}{一|yí}{句|jù}{话|huà}{概括|gài kuò}，{好|hǎo}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{不|bù}{只是|zhǐ shì}{知识|zhī shi}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{学习|xué xí}{的|de}{方法|fāng fǎ}。

({刚刚|gāng gāng}: only just; {公式|gōng shì} gōng shì: a formula; {初二|chū èr}: the second year of junior high.)
</details>

Checklist: Is there one scene told in detail? Do {渐渐|jiàn jiàn}, {后来|hòu lái}, {开始|kāi shǐ}…{可是|kě shì}…, {更|gèng}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{是|shì} show how things changed?
Does the last paragraph sum up in one sentence?

## Say it

```speak
# School and university
{我|wǒ}{通常|tōng cháng}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}，{今天|jīn tiān}{起|qǐ}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}。
= I usually get up at seven; today I overslept.
{天|tiān}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{冷|lěng}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{回去|huí qù}{吧|ba}。
= It's getting colder: let's go back.
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{一|yì}{所|suǒ}{很|hěn}{有名|yǒu míng}{的|de}{大学|dà xué}。
= This is a well-known university.
{她|tā}{是|shì}{中文|Zhōng wén}{系|xì}{的|de}{学生|xué sheng}，2030{届|jiè}{毕业|bì yè}。
= She's a student in the Chinese department, graduating in 2030.
{作业|zuò yè}{多|duō}{得|de}{数|shǔ}{不|bu}{清|qīng}。
= There's more homework than you could count.
{论文|lùn wén}{初稿|chū gǎo}{四|sì}{月|yuè}{底|dǐ}{以前|yǐ qián}{提交|tí jiāo}。
= The first draft of the thesis is due by the end of April.
```

## Pronunciation

- {数|shǔ} shǔ (to count) and {数|shù} shù (a number): {数一数|shǔ yi shǔ} shǔ yi shǔ, {数学|shù xué} shù xué.
- {={系|xì}=} xì (a department) is fourth tone, as in {关系|guān xi}; {={系|jì}=} jì (to tie, lesson 15) has another initial too.
- {届|jiè} jiè and {及格|jí gé} jí gé: j, with lips spread, not English "j".
- {哲学|zhé xué} zhé xué: zh (tongue curled back), then x (tongue flat). {物理|wù lǐ} wù lǐ, {地理|dì lǐ} dì lǐ: the same {理|lǐ} lǐ.
- {宿舍|sù shè} sù shè: s, then sh. Take care not to say shù shè.
- {橡皮|xiàng pí} xiàng pí: 4+2.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{往往|wǎng wǎng}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}~~: {往往|wǎng wǎng} isn't for the future or plans: {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{去|qù}{图书馆|tú shū guǎn}.
- ~~{请|qǐng}{渐渐|jiàn jiàn}{说|shuō}~~: {渐渐|jiàn jiàn} is change by itself, not speed: {请|qǐng}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{说|shuō}.
- {一|yì}{家|jiā}{大学|dà xué} is heard, but in writing schools take {所|suǒ} ({一|yì}{所|suǒ}{大学|dà xué}); {家|jiā} is for companies and shops.
- {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{学|xué}{数学|shù xué}{系|xì} sounds odd: you study a {专业|zhuān yè} and are in a {={系|xì}=}: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{上|shàng}{数学|shù xué}{系|xì}, or {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{学|xué}{数学|shù xué}{专业|zhuān yè}.
- In {他|tā}{数|shǔ}{了|le}{数|shǔ}{这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}{的|de}{页数|yè shù} (he counted the pages of the book), the verb {数|shǔ} is shǔ, third tone; only {页数|yè shù} (the number of pages) has shù.

## Key points

- {通常|tōng cháng}: usually (the normal case; also "usual" before a noun). {时常|shí cháng}: often (written). {往往|wǎng wǎng}: tends to,
  under a condition, not for plans. {经常|jīng cháng} / {常常|cháng cháng}: often.
- {渐渐|jiàn jiàn} ({地|de}): gradually, change by itself. {慢|màn}{慢|màn} (spoken), {逐渐|zhú jiàn} (written, lesson 22).
- {一|yì}{所|suǒ}{大学|dà xué} / {医院|yī yuàn}; {第|dì}{十|shí}{届|jiè}, 2030{届|jiè}, {本|běn}{届|jiè} / {上|shàng}{一|yí}{届|jiè} / {下|xià}{一|yí}{届|jiè}.
- {={系|xì}=} xì: a department ({系|xì}{主任|zhǔ rèn}); {数|shǔ} shǔ: to count ({数|shǔ}{不|bu}{清|qīng}); {才|cái} cái: talent ({很|hěn}{有才|yǒu cái}).
- School subjects ({语文|yǔ wén}, {地理|dì lǐ}, {物理|wù lǐ}, {化学|huà xué}, {哲学|zhé xué}, {政治|zhèng zhì}), university ({学年|xué nián}, {学分|xué fēn}, {论文|lùn wén}, {讲座|jiǎng zuò}, {学术|xué shù}, {学者|xué zhě}), exams ({试卷|shì juàn},
  {题目|tí mù}, {填|tián}, {及格|jí gé}, {录取|lù qǔ}, {难度|nán dù}, {初级|chū jí} / {中级|zhōng jí} / {高级|gāo jí}).
- New characters: {尺|chǐ}✎ {革|gé} {渐|jiàn} {铃|líng} {届|jiè} {勤|qín} {卷|juàn} {宿|sù}✎ {橡|xiàng} {幼|yòu} {哲|zhé} {政|zhèng}✎; new radical {=幺=}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Talking about language
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've been learning Chinese for five courses; this lesson gives you the words to talk about it:
sounds, letters, words, meanings, style and the {成语|chéng yǔ} (idioms) that begin at this level. {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna),
who guides visitors at a museum, has to explain Chinese to people who don't speak it, and you'll
see how she does it. You'll learn:

- the emphatic {可|kě}: {你|nǐ}{可|kě}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le} (mind you don't forget), {这儿|zhèr}{可|kě}{好|hǎo}{了|le} (it's really lovely here);
- {绝对|jué duì} (absolutely) and {的确|dí què} (indeed, it's true that);
- {称为|chēng wéi} (to be called, written) beside {叫作|jiào zuò};
- the noun **[[suffix]]** {头|tou}, said tou in the neutral tone ({石头|shí tou}, {木头|mù tou}, {里头|lǐ tou});
- what an **[[idiom]]** ({成语|chéng yǔ}) is, and how to talk about one: {出自|chū zì} (comes from), {比喻|bǐ yù} (a figure of speech).

## The emphatic {可|kě}

You know {可|kě} from {可以|kě yǐ} and {可是|kě shì}. On its own before a verb or an adjective, {可|kě} adds emphasis, in
speech. It has three common jobs.

**Warnings and reminders**, with {别|bié} / {不要|bú yào} / {要|yào} / {得|de}:

{明天|míng tiān}{的|de}{讲座|jiǎng zuò}{你|nǐ}{可|kě}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！ — Mind you don't forget tomorrow's lecture!

{外面|wài miàn}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{可|kě}{要|yào}{小心|xiǎo xīn}。 — It's raining outside: do be careful.

**"Really", with {了|le} (or {啦|la} la, a spoken {了|le} + {啊|a}) at the end**, often about how good or bad something is:

{这|zhè}{家|jiā}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{的|de}{菜|cài}{可|kě}{好吃|hǎo chī}{了|le}！ — The food at this restaurant is really good!

{他|tā}{的|de}{书法|shū fǎ}{可|kě}{漂亮|piào liang}{了|le}。 — His calligraphy is really beautiful.

**"Certainly, after all"**, against what someone thinks:

{这个|zhè ge}{问题|wèn tí}{可|kě}{不|bù}{简单|jiǎn dān}。 — This question is certainly not simple.

{我|wǒ}{可|kě}{没|méi}{说|shuō}{过|guo}{这|zhè}{句|jù}{话|huà}！ — I never said that!

The emphatic {可|kě} carries no meaning of "can": {你|nǐ}{可|kě}{别|bié}{去|qù} is "mind you don't go", not "you
may not go". It belongs to conversation; in writing, say {一定|yí dìng} ({一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{小心|xiǎo xīn}) or {非常|fēi cháng} ({非常|fēi cháng}{好吃|hǎo chī}).

## {绝对|jué duì} and {的确|dí què}

{绝对|jué duì} is "absolutely". Before a verb it makes a promise or a strong claim; before {不|bù} / {没|méi} it rules
something out:

{你|nǐ}{放心|fàng xīn}，{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{绝对|jué duì}{准时|zhǔn shí}{到|dào}。 — Don't worry: I'll definitely be on time tomorrow.

{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{绝对|jué duì}{不|bù}{能|néng}{告诉|gào su}{别人|bié ren}。 — You absolutely must not tell anyone about this.

It's an adjective too: {没有|méi yǒu}{绝对|jué duì}{的|de}{标准|biāo zhǔn} (there's no absolute standard).

{的确|dí què} (dí què: {的|de} is dí here) is "indeed, it's true that": it confirms something said or expected:

{你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{对|duì}，{汉字|hàn zì}{的确|dí què}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}{写|xiě}。 — You're right: characters really are hard to write.

{这|zhè}{本|běn}{词典|cí diǎn}{的确|dí què}{很|hěn}{有用|yǒu yòng}。 — This dictionary really is very useful.

{的确|dí què} and HSK 4's {确实|què shí} mean the same as adverbs; only {确实|què shí} is also an adjective ({确实|què shí}{的|de}{消息|xiāo xi}, reliable
news). Use {的确|dí què} when you agree: A: {汉字|hàn zì}{很|hěn}{难|nán}{写|xiě}。B: {的确|dí què}{是|shì}{这样|zhè yàng}。 (That's true.)

## {称为|chēng wéi}: to be called (written)

{称为|chēng wéi} is the written partner of HSK 4's {叫作|jiào zuò}. It comes in two frames:

- A {被|bèi}{称为|chēng wéi} B (A is called B): {景德镇|Jǐng dé zhèn}{被|bèi}{称为|chēng wéi}"{瓷都|cí dū}"。 (Jingdezhen is called "the porcelain capital": lesson 10h1.) /
  {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{写法|xiě fǎ}{被|bèi}{称为|chēng wéi}"{书法|shū fǎ}"。
- {把|bǎ} A {称为|chēng wéi} B (we call A B): {人们|rén men}{把|bǎ}{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{瓷器|cí qì}{称为|chēng wéi}"{青花瓷|qīng huā cí}"。 — People call this kind of porcelain
  "blue-and-white".

In written definitions {被|bèi} is often left out: {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{字|zì}{称为|chēng wéi}"{形声字|xíng shēng zì}" (characters of this kind are called
phonetic compounds). With the namer as subject, use lesson 12's {称|chēng}…{为|wéi}…: {我们|wǒ men}{称|chēng}{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{汉字|hàn zì}{为|wéi}"{简体字|jiǎn tǐ zì}" (we call
these characters "simplified"). In speech, {叫|jiào} or {叫作|jiào zuò} does the same job: {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{瓷器|cí qì}
{叫|jiào}{青花瓷|qīng huā cí}.

## The suffix {头|tou}

{头|tóu} tóu is "head" (HSK 2). As a **[[suffix]]** it loses its tone and its meaning, and simply makes a noun:

| Word | Meaning | Made from |
|---|---|---|
| {石头|shí tou} | stone | {石|shí} (stone) |
| {木头|mù tou} | wood | {木|mù} (tree, wood) |
| {馒头|mán tou} | steamed bun | (HSK 4) |
| {里头|lǐ tou} / {外头|wài tou} | inside / outside | {里|lǐ} / {外|wài} |
| {前头|qián tou} / {后头|hòu tou} / {上头|shàng tou} | in front / behind / above | {前|qián} / {后|hòu} / {上|shàng} |

The locative ones ({里头|lǐ tou}, {外头|wài tou}, {前头|qián tou}…) are spoken partners of {里面|lǐ miàn}, {外面|wài miàn}, {前面|qián miàn}. Say all of them with a light
tou: shí tou, mù tou, lǐ tou. A spoken pattern you'll hear: verb + {头|tou} for "worth doing": {这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}{没|méi}{什么|shén me}
{看头|kàn tou} (this film isn't worth watching). Lesson 22 has {石头|shí tou} as its own word; the suffix is what they
share.

## Idioms: {成语|chéng yǔ}

An **[[idiom]]** ({成语|chéng yǔ} chéng yǔ, HSK 6's word) is a set phrase, almost always of four characters, whose
meaning goes beyond its parts and which often comes from an old story or text. You've already met a
few at this level: {各行各业|gè háng gè yè} (every trade and profession, lesson 01), {五颜六色|wǔ yán liù sè} (all the colours,
lesson 10), {亲朋好友|qīn péng hǎo yǒu} (friends and relatives, lesson 15). Talking about one, you'll need:

- {出自|chū zì} (to come from a source): {这个|zhè ge}{成语|chéng yǔ}{出自|chū zì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{古代|gǔ dài}{的|de}{故事|gù shi}。 — This idiom comes from an old story
  ({古代|gǔ dài}, ancient times, is lesson 25's word).
- {比喻|bǐ yù} (a figure of speech; to use as a figure for): "{画蛇添足|huà shé tiān zú}"{比喻|bǐ yù}{做|zuò}{了|le}{多余|duō yú}{的|de}{事|shì}。 — {画蛇添足|huà shé tiān zú} ("drawing feet on a
  snake") is a figure for doing something unnecessary ({多余|duō yú}: superfluous).
- {形容|xíng róng} (to describe, to be used of): "{五颜六色|wǔ yán liù sè}"{形容|xíng róng}{颜色|yán sè}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — {五颜六色|wǔ yán liù sè} describes lots of colours.
- {意味着|yì wèi zhe} (to mean, to imply): {学|xué}{会|huì}{用|yòng}{成语|chéng yǔ}，{意味着|yì wèi zhe}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{更|gèng}{地道|dì dao}{了|le}。 — Learning to use idioms means your
  Chinese is becoming more natural ({地道|dì dao} dì dao: authentic, natural, HSK 6).

The honors lessons of this module tell three of the stories behind famous idioms (lesson 20h1) and
look at how idioms are built and used (20h2); the reference sheet lists the level's idioms.

## Words for language

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| Sounds | {拼音|pīn yīn} (pinyin), {字母|zì mǔ} (a letter of an alphabet), {发音|fā yīn} (pronunciation; to pronounce), {读音|dú yīn} (the reading of a character), {语音|yǔ yīn} (speech sounds; a voice message), {语气|yǔ qì} (tone of voice, mood) |
| Words and meaning | {词汇|cí huì} (vocabulary), {用法|yòng fǎ} (usage), {意义|yì yì} (meaning, significance), {意味着|yì wèi zhe} (to mean, imply), {认|rèn} (to recognise: {认|rèn}{字|zì}, {认|rèn}{出来|chū lái}) |
| Describing | {形容|xíng róng} (to describe; used of), {描述|miáo shù} (to describe, give an account of), {比喻|bǐ yù} (figure of speech), {生动|shēng dòng} (vivid, lively), {表达|biǎo dá} (to express), {表明|biǎo míng} (to show, make clear) |

{适用|shì yòng} + {于|yú}).

1. What is the main point of the text?
2. How does Anna now answer "how many characters are there"?
3. How does she explain tones?
4. What does the last sentence suggest?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Explaining Chinese to people who don't speak it works best with examples and comparisons that
   link to what they already know, not with rules.
2. About three thousand characters are in common use, and with those you can read a newspaper
   ({常用|cháng yòng}{的|de}{汉字|hàn zì}{大约|dà yuē}{有|yǒu}{三千|sān qiān}{个|gè}).
3. By pointing out that English has something similar: one word said in different tones of voice
   ({真|zhēn}{的|de} can show surprise or doubt); Chinese just puts this change on every syllable.
4. That the lesson she learned (connect new knowledge to what people already know) is true of
   teaching and explaining in general, not only of Chinese.

"**How to explain Chinese to foreign friends.** I've been a guide at the museum for half a year now.
Foreign visitors often ask me questions about Chinese. At first I always wanted to explain the
grammar perfectly clearly, and after a long explanation they still looked puzzled. Later I found
that for people who have never learned Chinese, examples work better than rules. For instance,
someone asks 'How many Chinese characters are there?' I used to say 'about several tens of
thousands', and everyone was shocked and thought Chinese was too hard to learn. Now I put it another
way: 'About three thousand characters are in common use; once you know those three thousand,
reading a newspaper isn't too hard.' The same meaning in a different form, and the listeners
feel completely differently. Or again, many people find tones hard. I tell them that English has
something similar: the same word said in a different tone of voice means something different. 'Really'
can show surprise, or doubt. Chinese just puts that kind of change on every syllable. Put like that,
everyone understands at once. I've also learned to use comparisons. I say characters are a bit
like building blocks: a character is made of several parts; some show the meaning and some the
sound. The more parts you know, the easier new characters become. It's a vivid comparison, and even
children understand it. Of course, sometimes I can't explain things clearly. Once a visitor asked me what {了|le} means. I thought it over and over, and in the end could only tell him that {了|le} has several uses and we'd talk about it next time. When I got home I looked it up carefully, and the next day I wrote a few examples on a sheet of paper and gave it to him. What I've learned most in these six months is that explaining a language
isn't just passing on knowledge: more importantly, you have to find something the listener knows
already and connect the new knowledge to it. I think that holds for more than explaining Chinese."
</details>

## Write it: a picture story

Four pictures, 100–150 characters.

1. A foreign visitor at a fruit stall points at some pears.
2. She says a word, and the stall-keeper hands her a bag of chestnuts instead.
3. She takes out her phone and shows him the characters.
4. They both laugh; she buys the pears and writes the tones in her notebook.

<details>
<summary>Model story</summary>

{玛莎|Mǎ shā}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{不久|bù jiǔ}。{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{她|tā}{去|qù}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}{店|diàn}{买|mǎi}{梨|lí}。{她|tā}{指|zhǐ}{着|zhe}{梨|lí}{对|duì}{老板|lǎo bǎn}{说|shuō}："{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{两|liǎng}{斤|jīn}'{栗子|lì zi}'。"{老板|lǎo bǎn}{听|tīng}{了|le}，{给|gěi}{了|le}{她|tā}{一|yí}{袋|dài}{栗子|lì zi}。{玛莎|Mǎ shā}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{奇怪|qí guài}，{就|jiù}{拿|ná}{出|chū}{手机|shǒu jī}，{把|bǎ}"{梨|lí}"{字|zì}{给|gěi}{老板|lǎo bǎn}{看|kàn}。{老板|lǎo bǎn}{这|zhè}{才|cái}{明白|míng bai}，{原来|yuán lái}{她|tā}{把|bǎ}"{梨|lí}"{的|de}{读音|dú yīn}{说|shuō}{错|cuò}{了|le}。{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{笑|xiào}{了|le}{起来|qǐ lái}。{回|huí}{家|jiā}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{玛莎|Mǎ shā}{在|zài}{本子|běn zi}{上|shàng}{认真|rèn zhēn}{地|de}{写|xiě}{下|xià}{了|le}"{梨|lí} lí"{和|hé}"{栗|lì} lì"，{她|tā}{说|shuō}："{一|yí}{个|gè}{声调|shēng diào}，{意义|yì yì}{就|jiù}{完全|wán quán}{不同|bù tóng}{了|le}。"

({栗子|lì zi} lì zi: chestnuts; {斤|jīn}: half a kilo, HSK 4; {指|zhǐ}{着|zhe}: pointing at.)
</details>

## Write it: the hardest thing about Chinese

Write 200–300 characters: what you find hardest about Chinese, an example, what you do about it,
and what it has taught you. Use {的确|dí què}, {绝对|jué duì} or {可|kě} (in reported speech), and one of {形容|xíng róng} / {表达|biǎo dá} / {比喻|bǐ yù}.

<details>
<summary>Model essay</summary>

{对|duì}{我|wǒ}{来|lái}{说|shuō}，{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{最|zuì}{难|nán}{的|de}{不|bú}{是|shì}{语法|yǔ fǎ}，{而|ér}{是|shì}{声调|shēng diào}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}{常常|cháng cháng}{说|shuō}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{语法|yǔ fǎ}{没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}，{可是|kě shì}{一|yì}{开口|kāi kǒu}，{中国|Zhōng guó}{朋友|péng you}{有时候|yǒu shí hou}{就|jiù}{听|tīng}{不|bu}{懂|dǒng}。

{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{次|cì}，{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{想|xiǎng}{说|shuō}"{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{汤|tāng}"，{结果|jié guǒ}{说|shuō}{成|chéng}{了|le}"{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{糖|táng}"，{服务员|fú wù yuán}{一脸|yì liǎn}{吃惊|chī jīng}。{从|cóng}{那|nà}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{我|wǒ}{开始|kāi shǐ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{练习|liàn xí}{声调|shēng diào}。{我|wǒ}{用|yòng}{手机|shǒu jī}{把|bǎ}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{发音|fā yīn}{录|lù}{下来|xià lái}，{跟|gēn}{老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{读音|dú yīn}{比较|bǐ jiào}，{找|zhǎo}{出|chū}{不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}{的|de}{地方|dì fang}，{再|zài}{反复|fǎn fù}{练|liàn}。{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{用|yòng}{手|shǒu}{的|de}{动作|dòng zuò}{帮助|bāng zhù}{记忆|jì yì}：{第|dì}{一|yī}{声|shēng}{手|shǒu}{平|píng}{着|zhe}{走|zǒu}，{第|dì}{四|sì}{声|shēng}{手|shǒu}{往|wǎng}{下|xià}{走|zǒu}。

{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{发音|fā yīn}{的确|dí què}{好|hǎo}{多|duō}{了|le}，{虽然|suī rán}{有时候|yǒu shí hou}{还|hái}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{错|cuò}，{但是|dàn shì}{大|dà}{部分|bù fen}{时候|shí hou}{别人|bié ren}{都|dōu}{能|néng}{听|tīng}{懂|dǒng}。{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{明白|míng bai}，{学|xué}{语言|yǔ yán}{不|bù}{能|néng}{只|zhǐ}{看|kàn}{书|shū}，{还|hái}{要|yào}{多|duō}{开口|kāi kǒu}，{不|bú}{怕|pà}{出错|chū cuò}。{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{这个|zhè ge}{道理|dào li}{不|bù}{只|zhǐ}{适用|shì yòng}{于|yú}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。

({录|lù}{下来|xià lái}: to record it, lesson 20's {录|lù}; {出错|chū cuò}: to make mistakes.)
</details>

Checklist: Is the example a real scene? Does the middle paragraph say what you do, step by step? Is
there a sentence that sums up ({这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{明白|míng bai}…)?

## Say it

```speak
# Talking about language
{明天|míng tiān}{的|de}{讲座|jiǎng zuò}{你|nǐ}{可|kě}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！
= Mind you don't forget tomorrow's lecture!
{你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{对|duì}，{汉字|hàn zì}{的确|dí què}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}{写|xiě}。
= You're right: characters really are hard to write.
{放心|fàng xīn}，{我|wǒ}{绝对|jué duì}{准时|zhǔn shí}{到|dào}。
= Don't worry, I'll definitely be on time.
{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{写法|xiě fǎ}{被|bèi}{称为|chēng wéi}{书法|shū fǎ}。
= This way of writing is called calligraphy.
{这个|zhè ge}{成语|chéng yǔ}{出自|chū zì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{古代|gǔ dài}{的|de}{故事|gù shi}。
= This idiom comes from an old story.
{这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{字|zì}{的|de}{发音|fā yīn}{很|hěn}{相似|xiāng sì}。
= These two characters sound alike.
```

## Pronunciation

- {的确|dí què} dí què: {的|de} is dí here (as in {目的|mù dì} mù dì it's dì). Not de.
- {逻辑|luó jí} luó jí; {词汇|cí huì} cí huì; {比喻|bǐ yù} bǐ yù (3+4).
- The suffix {头|tou} is neutral: {石头|shí tou} shí tou, {木头|mù tou} mù tou, {里头|lǐ tou} lǐ tou. {头|tóu} tóu (head) keeps its rising tone.
- {意义|yì yì} yì yì: two fourth tones, two different characters. {意思|yì si} yì si (HSK 2) ends in a neutral tone.
- {念|niàn} niàn and {认|rèn} rèn: n- and r-, both fourth tone.
- {演讲|yǎn jiǎng} yǎn jiǎng: two third tones, so the first is said as a rising tone (yán jiǎng); it's still
  written yǎn.

## Common mistakes

- {这个|zhè ge}{问题|wèn tí}{可|kě}{简单|jiǎn dān} sounds unfinished: the "really" {可|kě} wants {了|le} at the end: {这个|zhè ge}{问题|wèn tí}{可|kě}{简单|jiǎn dān}{了|le}.
- ~~{的确|dí què}{的|de}{消息|xiāo xi}~~: {的确|dí què} is only an adverb; the adjective is {确实|què shí}: {确实|què shí}{的|de}{消息|xiāo xi}.
- {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{字|zì}{很|hěn}{类似|lèi sì} is heard, but {类似|lèi sì} more often sits before a noun ({类似|lèi sì}{的|de}{字|zì}) or takes {于|yú}; for two things
  being alike, {相似|xiāng sì} is the usual word: {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{字|zì}{很|hěn}{相似|xiāng sì}.
- Saying {石头|shí tou} with a rising {头|tóu} (shí tóu): the suffix is light.

## Key points

- Emphatic {可|kě} (spoken): {可|kě}{别|bié} / {可|kě}{要|yào} (warnings), {可|kě} + adjective + {了|le} (really…), {可|kě}{不|bù} / {可|kě}{没|méi} (certainly not).
- {绝对|jué duì}: absolutely ({绝对|jué duì}{不行|bù xíng}; {绝对|jué duì}{的|de}{自由|zì yóu}). {的确|dí què} dí què: indeed (adverb only; {确实|què shí} is also an adjective).
- {称为|chēng wéi} (written): A {被|bèi}{称为|chēng wéi} B; {把|bǎ} A {称为|chēng wéi} B; spoken {叫|jiào} / {叫作|jiào zuò}.
- Suffix {头|tou}: {石头|shí tou}, {木头|mù tou}, {里头|lǐ tou}, {前头|qián tou}; light tone.
- {成语|chéng yǔ}: four-character set phrases; {出自|chū zì}, {比喻|bǐ yù}, {形容|xíng róng}, {意味着|yì wèi zhe} to talk about them.
- {发音|fā yīn} / {读音|dú yīn} / {语音|yǔ yīn}; {形容|xíng róng} / {描述|miáo shù}; {表达|biǎo dá} / {表明|biǎo míng}; {类似|lèi sì} / {相似|xiāng sì}.
- New characters: {喻|yù} {逻|luó} {辑|jí} {类|lèi}✎ {描|miáo} {述|shù} {形|xíng}✎ {义|yì}✎.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Science, technology and invention
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson reads and talks about science: research, experiments, data, machines and inventions.
{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (Wang Fang) interviews a researcher about a museum robot, and the reading is a short piece of
popular science about how memory works, the kind of text the HSK 5 reading paper likes. You'll learn:

- the **[[basis prepositions]]** {凭|píng} / {凭借|píng jiè} (by virtue of, on the strength of) and {依据|yī jù} (on the basis of), with
  a first look at {据|jù} and {据说|jù shuō} (according to; it is said: lesson 24);
- the suffix {化|huà} (-ise, -ify): {现代化|xiàn dài huà}, {智能化|zhì néng huà}, {简单化|jiǎn dān huà};
- the words of research ({科研|kē yán}, {实验|shí yàn}, {测试|cè shì}, {数据|shù jù}, {调研|diào yán}…), of technology ({系统|xì tǒng}, {程序|chéng xù}, {设备|shè bèi}, {智能|zhì néng}…) and of
  invention ({发明|fā míng}, {创新|chuàng xīn}, {创造|chuàng zào}, {成果|chéng guǒ}, {奇迹|qí jì}…).

The module's three-photo speaking task is near the end.

## {凭|píng} and {凭借|píng jiè}: by virtue of, on the strength of

{凭|píng} + a noun says what something rests on: what you show, what you rely on, what gives you the right.
It's one of the **[[basis prepositions]]**.

On notices, {凭|píng} is "on presentation of":

{凭|píng}{票|piào}{入场|rù chǎng}。 — Admission by ticket only.

{学生|xué sheng}{凭|píng}{学生证|xué sheng zhèng}{可以|kě yǐ}{免费|miǎn fèi}{参观|cān guān}。 — Students can visit free on showing a student card.

In a story, it's what someone relied on to succeed:

{她|tā}{凭|píng}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{努力|nǔ lì}，{考|kǎo}{上|shàng}{了|le}{一|yì}{所|suǒ}{好|hǎo}{大学|dà xué}。 — Through her own hard work she got into a good university.

{凭借|píng jiè} is the same idea, more written, and usually with a longer phrase: {这|zhè}{家|jiā}{公司|gōng sī}{凭借|píng jiè}{先进|xiān jìn}{的|de}{技术|jì shù}，{很|hěn}{快|kuài}{就|jiù}{发展|fā zhǎn}{起来|qǐ lái}{了|le}
(on the strength of its advanced technology, the company quickly grew). In a question, {凭|píng}{什么|shén me}
asks for someone's grounds: {你|nǐ}{凭|píng}{什么|shén me}{这么|zhè me}{说|shuō}？ (what grounds do you have for saying that?) is a challenge, so use it with care.

## {依据|yī jù}: on the basis of; grounds

{依据|yī jù} is a written, more formal {根据|gēn jù} (HSK 3). As a preposition it says what a decision or a
judgment follows:

{依据|yī jù}{学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{规定|guī dìng}，{考试|kǎo shì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{不|bù}{能|néng}{使用|shǐ yòng}{手机|shǒu jī}。 — Under the school's rules, phones may not be used in exams.

As a noun it's the grounds, the evidence for something: {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{说法|shuō fǎ}{没有|méi yǒu}{科学|kē xué}{依据|yī jù} (there's no scientific basis for
this claim); {你|nǐ}{的|de}{依据|yī jù}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}？ (what are your grounds?).

| Word | Register | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| {根据|gēn jù} | everyday and written | {根据|gēn jù}{地图|dì tú}，{我们|wǒ men}{应该|yīng gāi}{往|wǎng}{东|dōng}{走|zǒu}。 |
| {依据|yī jù} | written, formal | {依据|yī jù}{规定|guī dìng} / {法律|fǎ lǜ} / {数据|shù jù}; {科学|kē xué}{依据|yī jù} |
| {凭|píng} | everyday; notices | {凭|píng}{票|piào}{入场|rù chǎng}; {凭|píng}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{努力|nǔ lì} |
| {凭借|píng jiè} | written | {凭借|píng jiè}{先进|xiān jìn}{的|de}{技术|jì shù} |

**A preview: {据|jù} and {据说|jù shuō}.** {据|jù} is the shortest of the family: {据|jù}{调查|diào chá} (according to a survey), {据|jù}{报道|bào dào}
(according to reports, lesson 24). {据说|jù shuō} is "it is said, they say": {据说|jù shuō}{这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{机器人|jī qì rén}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{五|wǔ}{种|zhǒng}{语言|yǔ yán} (they say this robot
speaks five languages). Both are lesson 24's words; you'll see them often in news.

## The suffix {化|huà}: -ise, -ify

{化|huà} after an adjective or a noun makes a word for a process: becoming more so. It works like English
-ise or -ify:

| Word | Made from | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {现代化|xiàn dài huà} | {现代|xiàn dài} (modern, lesson 25) | modernisation; to modernise (lesson 21's word) |
| {智能化|zhì néng huà} | {智能|zhì néng} (intelligent) | becoming "smart" (of machines, homes) |
| {自动化|zì dòng huà} | {自动|zì dòng} (automatic, lesson 20) | automation |
| {简单化|jiǎn dān huà} | {简单|jiǎn dān} (simple) | simplification; to oversimplify |
| {国际化|guó jì huà} | {国际|guó jì} (international) | internationalisation |
| {多样化|duō yàng huà} | {多样|duō yàng} (varied) | diversification |

These words act as nouns ({实现|shí xiàn}{现代化|xiàn dài huà}, achieve modernisation) or as predicates ({城市|chéng shì}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{现代化|xiàn dài huà}{了|le}, the city is
getting more and more modern). {简单化|jiǎn dān huà} often criticises: {这个|zhè ge}{问题|wèn tí}{不|bù}{能|néng}{简单化|jiǎn dān huà} (don't oversimplify this problem).
In speech, {变|biàn}{得|de}{更|gèng}… often does the same job: {生活|shēng huó}{变|biàn}{得|de}{更|gèng}{方便|fāng biàn}{了|le}.

## Words for science and technology

**Research.** {科研|kē yán} (scientific research), {研发|yán fā} (research and development), {研制|yán zhì} (to develop, make: of a new
product or drug), {调研|diào yán} (to research and investigate, a survey on the ground), {实验|shí yàn} (an experiment: {做|zuò}{实验|shí yàn}),
{实验室|shí yàn shì} (a lab), {试验|shì yàn} (a trial, a test run: of a new method or machine), {测|cè} / {测试|cè shì} (to measure, test; a test),
{数据|shù jù} (data), {收集|shōu jí} (to collect: {收集|shōu jí}{数据|shù jù}), {问卷|wèn juàn} (a questionnaire: {做|zuò}{问卷|wèn juàn}{调查|diào chá}), {专家|zhuān jiā} (an expert), {领域|lǐng yù} (a field), {生物|shēng wù}
(living things; biology), {大脑|dà nǎo} (the brain).

{实验|shí yàn} shí yàn and {试验|shì yàn} shì yàn sound alike: {实验|shí yàn} tests an idea in a lab; {试验|shì yàn} tries out something new in
practice ({新|xīn}{药|yào}{的|de}{试验|shì yàn}, a trial of a new drug).

**Technology.** {系统|xì tǒng} (a system), {程序|chéng xù} (a procedure; a computer program), {操作|cāo zuò} (to operate; operation), {设备|shè bèi}
(equipment), {机器|jī qì} / {机器人|jī qì rén} (a machine / a robot), {计算机|jì suàn jī} (a computer: the formal word; {电脑|diàn nǎo} is the everyday
one), {人工|rén gōng} (artificial; by hand: {人工智能|rén gōng zhì néng}, artificial intelligence), {智能|zhì néng} (intelligent; smart: {智能|zhì néng}{手机|shǒu jī}),
{高科技|gāo kē jì} (high tech), {工程|gōng chéng} / {工程师|gōng chéng shī} (engineering, a project / an engineer).

**Invention and use.** {发明|fā míng} (to invent; an invention), {创新|chuàng xīn} (to innovate; innovation), {创造|chuàng zào} (to create), {制造|zhì zào} (to
